title: What complaints handling training does ASIC RG 271 require?
description: What ASIC RG 271 expects of complaints staff knowledge, skills and training, the IDR timeframes they must apply, and the evidence an auditor will ask for.
shortAnswer: Regulatory Guide 271 Internal dispute resolution, issued by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC), expects financial firms to give complaints staff targeted induction and ongoing training, to build the required knowledge and skills into position descriptions and performance assessments, and to train all staff on the IDR process. The training guidance itself is not an enforceable paragraph, but staffing, delegations, systemic issue escalation and the 30, 45 and 21 day response deadlines are.
keyTakeaways: RG 271 was issued on September 2, 2021 and applies to complaints received on or after October 5, 2021. Paragraphs highlighted in the guide, and the standards in ASIC Instrument 2020/98, are enforceable.
RG 271.148 to RG 271.150 set out the knowledge, skills and induction and ongoing training topics ASIC expects for complaints staff. These are guidance, not enforceable paragraphs.

Enforceable paragraphs that depend on capable staff include sufficient staffing within IDR timeframes (RG 271.143), authority to resolve complaints (RG 271.146 to RG 271.147) and escalation of systemic issues (RG 271.120).

Staff must apply maximum IDR response timeframes: 30 calendar days for standard complaints, 45 for trustee and most superannuation complaints, and 21 for credit complaints involving default or hardship notices.
ASIC expects all staff, not only complaints specialists, to be trained on the IDR process and to identify people who need help to complain.
appliesTo: Australian financial services (AFS) licensees, unlicensed product issuers and unlicensed secondary sellers
Trustees of regulated superannuation funds (other than SMSFs), approved deposit funds and RSA providers
Australian credit licensees and unlicensed carried over instrument lenders
Frontline staff, complaints officers, IDR managers, business unit managers and senior executives in those firms

sections.heading: Is complaints handling training mandatory under RG 271?

blocks.text: No paragraph of RG 271 makes training itself an enforceable requirement, but several enforceable paragraphs cannot be met without trained staff. The law requires most financial firms to have, and comply with, an internal dispute resolution (IDR) procedure that meets ASIC's standards: see section 912A(1)(g) of the Corporations Act 2001 and section 47(1)(h) of the National Consumer Credit Protection Act 2009, as cited in RG 271.1 and RG 271.2.

[RG 271](https://asic.gov.au/regulatory-resources/find-a-document/regulatory-guides/rg-271-internal-dispute-resolution/) distinguishes two kinds of content. RG 271.8 says the standards and requirements set out in ASIC Corporations, Credit and Superannuation (Internal Dispute Resolution) Instrument 2020/98 and highlighted in the guide "are enforceable". RG 271.9 says unhighlighted parts are guidance. The skills and training paragraphs (RG 271.148 to RG 271.150) are not highlighted, so they describe how ASIC expects firms to meet the enforceable outcomes rather than a freestanding duty.

In practice the distinction matters less than it appears. RG 271.143 (enforceable) requires staffing numbers sufficient to deal with complaints fairly and effectively within maximum IDR timeframes, RG 271.146 (enforceable) requires firms to give relevant staff appropriate authority to resolve complaints, and RG 271.120 (enforceable) requires firms to encourage and enable staff to escalate possible systemic issues. A firm that cannot show its people know how to do these things will struggle to show compliance. Training also sits within the broader duty to keep representatives adequately trained, described in [ASIC RG 105 organizational competence](/regulations/asic-rg-105-organisational-competence).

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: This page reflects RG 271 as issued on September 2, 2021, and ASIC's guide page as at November 2026. ASIC notes that AS/NZS 10002:2014, referred to throughout the guide, has been revised and reissued as AS 10002:2022.

sections.heading: Which staff does RG 271 expect to be trained?

blocks.text: RG 271 expects every staff member to understand the IDR process and complaints specialists to receive deeper, role specific training. RG 271.144 lists the people expected to play a role in a firm's IDR process: the chief executive (or equivalent) and senior management, the manager responsible for the IDR process, staff managing complaints, business unit managers, and frontline staff. RG 271.145 adds that all staff should understand their roles and responsibilities in relation to the IDR process.

items: **All staff:** RG 271.132(c) lists "providing training to all staff, not just complaints management staff, about the IDR process" as one way to make the process visible.

**Frontline staff:** RG 271.138 says firms should train staff to proactively identify, support and assist people who need help to make a complaint. RG 271.30 adds that a consumer does not need to use the word complaint or put it in writing to trigger the IDR obligations.
**Complaints management staff:** RG 271.150 sets out a targeted induction and ongoing training curriculum (see below).

**Boards and senior management:** RG 271.128 expects them to provide adequate resources, "including training and support to staff managing complaints", and RG 271.118 (enforceable) requires boards to set clear accountabilities for complaints handling and systemic issues.

sections.heading: What knowledge, skills and training topics does ASIC expect?

blocks.text: ASIC expects complaints staff to combine technical knowledge with communication and judgment. RG 271.148 lists knowledge of RG 271, consumer protection laws relating to financial products and services, Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA) approaches and relevant industry codes; an understanding of the firm's products and services; empathy, respect and courtesy; awareness of cultural differences and the ability to identify and assist complainants who need additional assistance; strong verbal and written communication; and analytical thinking and good judgment.

RG 271.149 says firms should write these skills and attributes into position descriptions, development plans and performance assessments for complaint management staff. RG 271.150 then lists topics that targeted induction and ongoing training may include:

items: the firm's IDR policy and process, including roles, responsibilities, authority and escalation points
financial services consumer protection laws, AFCA position statements and industry codes of practice
identifying and helping complainants who need additional assistance
effective communication and negotiation techniques, and effective written communications
complaint data capture and internal reporting
issues identification and analysis, and identifying and escalating possible systemic issues

blocks.text: Where a firm subscribes to an industry code, the code's own training commitments sit on top of RG 271. See the pages on the [Banking Code of Practice](/regulations/banking-code-of-practice-staff-training), [general insurance claims handling](/regulations/general-insurance-claims-handling-training) and the [Life Insurance Code of Practice](/regulations/life-insurance-code-of-practice-staff-training).

sections.heading: Which IDR timeframes must complaints staff be trained to apply?

blocks.text: Staff must know the maximum time allowed for an IDR response for each complaint type, because missing it is a breach of an enforceable paragraph. RG 271.56 says a firm "must provide an IDR response to a complainant no later than 30 calendar days after receiving the complaint", subject to the different timeframes in Table 2 and limited exceptions. Day 1 is the first day after receipt, applying section 36 of the Acts Interpretation Act 1901.

blocks.text: Staff also need to recognize what counts as a complaint. RG 271.27 adopts the AS/NZS 10002:2014 definition, RG 271.31 says firms should not treat a complaint as feedback or an inquiry merely because it was made verbally, because the firm thinks it lacks merit, or because a goodwill payment resolved it, and RG 271.32 (enforceable) brings in posts on a firm's own social media channels where the author is identifiable and contactable.

sections.heading: What must staff know about escalating systemic issues?

blocks.text: Staff must know how to raise a possible systemic issue from a single complaint, because RG 271.120 makes that pathway enforceable. Firms must encourage and enable staff to escalate possible systemic issues they identify from individual complaints, regularly analyze complaint data sets, promptly escalate possible systemic issues for investigation and action, and report internally on investigation outcomes in a timely way.

RG 271.119 adds that where a firm reports to its board or executive committees, the reports must include metrics and analysis of consumer complaints, including systemic issues identified through them. RG 271.121 expects prompt identification and fair remediation of affected consumers once a systemic issue is confirmed. Training for complaints staff should therefore include worked examples of patterns that should be escalated, and the escalation route should be tested, not just described.

sections.heading: How can a firm evidence complaints training to ASIC?

blocks.text: The strongest evidence links each person's role, the RG 271 expectation, the training delivered and a check of applied competence. ASIC's own paragraphs point to the records: position descriptions, development plans and performance assessments that reflect the RG 271.148 skills (RG 271.149); adequate materials such as scripts, checklists, sample letters and templates (RG 271.151); and a regular review of whether the IDR process is adequately resourced (RG 271.142, enforceable).

Because timeliness is measurable, complaint data is also training evidence. RG 271.189 to RG 271.190 expect regular compliance audits, at least annually unless complaint numbers are very small, and where non-compliance is found, "performance feedback, re-training and enhanced supervision" for complaints staff. Firms that serve retail clients also submit IDR data to ASIC every six months under ASIC Instrument 2022/205, and ASIC's [IDR data reporting page](https://asic.gov.au/regulatory-resources/financial-services/dispute-resolution/internal-dispute-resolution-data-reporting/) notes an updated handbook applying to complaints received or closed from January 1, 2026. Late responses and misclassified complaints in that data identify who needs retraining. The guide on [preparing training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit) sets out a register structure, and [financial services](/industries/financial-services) covers the wider obligation set.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models RG 271's paragraphs, the complaint types and their timeframes, and each IDR role as a structured framework, then links every role to the concepts and assessment points it must demonstrate. When ASIC updates the guide or a firm changes its delegations, the affected roles and assessments are identified from the framework, and each person's record shows which version they were assessed against.

faqs.q: Does RG 271 set a minimum number of training hours for complaints staff?
faqs.a: No. RG 271 sets no hours or fixed refresher interval. It expects targeted induction and ongoing training for complaints staff (RG 271.150) and IDR process training for all staff (RG 271.132(c)), and leaves the design to the firm. Firms should be able to justify their intervals against complaint volumes, error rates and changes to products or law.

faqs.q: Is acknowledging a complaint within 24 hours a legal requirement?
faqs.a: RG 271.51 says ASIC expects acknowledgement within 24 hours (or one business day) of receipt, or as soon as practicable. That paragraph is not highlighted as enforceable. The 30, 45, 21 and 90 day maximum IDR response timeframes in Table 2 are enforceable, so training should treat them as hard deadlines.

faqs.q: Do outsourced complaints teams need the same training?
faqs.a: RG 271.21 allows firms to outsource part or all of their IDR process, but RG 271.46 says the firm remains responsible for the provider's compliance with the guide. RG 271.48 (enforceable) requires due skill and care in choosing providers, ongoing performance monitoring and action on shortfalls, so the firm should hold evidence of the provider's training and quality checks.

faqs.q: Does RG 271 still refer to the 2014 complaints standard?
faqs.a: Yes. RG 271 refers to AS/NZS 10002:2014, including for the definition of complaint. ASIC's guide page notes that the standard was revised and reissued as AS 10002:2022, but RG 271 itself has not been reissued, so firms should train on the RG 271 definition.
